content: Cholestasis is a medical condition characterized by the inability of bile to flow from the liver to the duodenum. Bile production is a critical secretory function of the liver. It begins in small channels called bile canaliculi, which are formed between adjacent surfaces of liver cells, or hepatocytes. These canaliculi resemble the terminal branches of a tree. They merge to form larger structures, sometimes referred to as the Canals of Hering. These canals then connect to small bile ductules, which are lined with epithelial cells. The ductules further join to form bile ducts, which eventually converge into the right and left main hepatic ducts. The right hepatic duct drains bile from the right lobe of the liver, while the left hepatic duct drains bile from the left lobe. These two ducts unite to form the common hepatic duct, which subsequently joins the cystic duct from the gallbladder to create the common bile duct. The common bile duct then empties into the duodenum at the ampulla of Vater. Cholestasis can be classified into two main types. The first is obstructive cholestasis, which occurs when there is a mechanical blockage in the bile duct system. This can result from conditions such as gallstones or malignancies. The second type is metabolic cholestasis, which arises from disturbances in bile formation. These disturbances may be due to genetic defects or acquired conditions, such as side effects from certain medications. On a microscopic level, hepatocytes in cholestasis exhibit a brownish-green stippled appearance within their cytoplasm. This appearance is due to the accumulation of bile that cannot exit the cells. Additionally, bile plugs may be observed within the canaliculi between hepatocytes or within bile ducts. These plugs represent bile that has been excreted by the hepatocytes but is unable to progress further due to obstruction. This leads to the leakage of bile into the surrounding liver tissue, resulting in areas of hepatic necrosis. These necrotic areas, known as bile lakes, are typically associated with extra-hepatic bile duct obstruction. Laboratory findings in cholestasis often reveal elevated levels of bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase in the blood. These abnormalities reflect the impaired bile flow and the associated liver dysfunction.
